import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 8.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity (law) is a word $w$ in the free group on the letters $x_0, x_1, \ldots$;
a group $G$ satisfies it if $w = 1$ holds for every substitution of elements of $G$ for
the letters. The variety defined by $w$ is the class of all groups satisfying $w = 1$,
and its subvarieties are the varieties (classes of groups defined by a set of identities)
contained in it.

The algorithm receives the identity as a word, i.e. a list of letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$,
encoded as `List (ℕ × Bool)`, and `FreeGroup.mk` sends such a word to the element of
the free group it represents. The classes of groups range over groups in `Type`; since a
variety is determined by its laws, and a law fails in some group of a variety if and only
if it fails in a countable group of that variety, this loses nothing.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

/-- A word `w` in the free group on the countably many letters $x_0, x_1, \ldots$ is a
*law* (identity) of the group `G` if $w = 1$ holds identically in `G`, i.e. every
homomorphism `FreeGroup ℕ →* G` (every substitution of elements of `G` for the letters)
sends `w` to `1`. -/
def IsLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) (G : Type*) [Group G] : Prop :=
  ∀ f : FreeGroup ℕ →* G, f w = 1

/-- A class of groups `𝒞` is a *variety of groups* if it is the class of all groups
satisfying some set `S` of laws. -/
def IsVariety (𝒞 : (G : Type) → [Group G] → Prop) : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ), ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝒞 G ↔ ∀ w ∈ S, IsLaw w G

/-- The variety of groups defined by the identity $w = 1$: the class of all groups in
which `w` is a law. -/
def varietyOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : (G : Type) → [Group G] → Prop :=
  fun G _ => IsLaw w G

/-- The set of subvarieties of the variety defined by the identity $w = 1$, i.e. the
varieties of groups contained in it. -/
def subvarietiesOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Set ((G : Type) → [Group G] → Prop) :=
  {𝒰 | IsVariety 𝒰 ∧ ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝒰 G → varietyOfLaw w G}

/-- Every abelian group satisfies the commutator identity $[x_0, x_1] = 1$. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem isLaw_commutator (G : Type*) [CommGroup G] :
    IsLaw ⁅FreeGroup.of 0, FreeGroup.of 1⁆ G := fun f => by
  rw [map_commutatorElement, commutatorElement_eq_one_iff_mul_comm]
  exact mul_comm _ _

/-- The variety defined by an identity is a variety. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem isVariety_varietyOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : IsVariety (varietyOfLaw w) :=
  ⟨{w}, fun _ _ => by simp [varietyOfLaw]⟩

/-- The variety defined by an identity is a subvariety of itself. -/
@[category API, AMS 8 20]
theorem varietyOfLaw_mem_subvarietiesOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) :
    varietyOfLaw w ∈ subvarietiesOfLaw w :=
  ⟨isVariety_varietyOfLaw w, fun _ _ h => h⟩

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

That is, is the predicate on words `w` (over the letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$, given as
`List (ℕ × Bool)`) "the variety of groups defined by the identity $w = 1$ has at most
countably many subvarieties" a computable predicate?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun w : List (ℕ × Bool) =>
      (subvarietiesOfLaw (FreeGroup.mk w)).Countable := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«8.25»
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition is correct; the file follows the note's reading (one group word, ComputablePred, varieties determined by their laws, cardinality ≤ ℵ₀, answer(True) = algorithm exists).
modeling_decisions: Input encoding: the identity is presented as a word `List (ℕ × Bool)` (letter `(i, true)` = x_i, `(i, false)` = x_i⁻¹) sent to `FreeGroup ℕ` by `FreeGroup.mk`, rather than as an element of `FreeGroup ℕ` directly, because Mathlib has no `Primcodable (FreeGroup ℕ)` instance (constructing one would require proving primitive recursiveness of word reduction). Since word reduction is computable and the predicate factors through `FreeGroup.mk`, this is equivalent to decidability on (reduced) free-group elements.
A law is defined as `∀ f : FreeGroup ℕ →* G, f w = 1` (every substitution of elements of G for the letters kills w); this is the standard notion of a group satisfying the identity w = 1.

A variety is defined as a class of groups that is exactly the class of all groups satisfying some set of laws (the equational definition; equivalent to Birkhoff's HSP characterisation). Classes of groups are predicates `(G : Type) → [Group G] → Prop`, i.e. they range over groups in universe `Type` only. This does not change the number of subvarieties: a variety is determined by its set of laws, and a law fails in some group of a variety iff it fails in a countable (hence `Type`-sized) group of the variety, so the correspondence between varieties over all universes and `Type`-level varieties is bijective.
Subvarieties of V(w) are all varieties 𝒰 with 𝒰 ⊆ V(w), including V(w) itself and the trivial variety; this does not affect countability.
'At most countably many' is `Set.Countable`, i.e. cardinality ≤ ℵ₀ (finite or countably infinite).

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 8.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity (law) is an equation $w = 1$, where $w$ is a word in the variables
$x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$, i.e. an element of the free group $F_\infty$ of countably infinite rank.
A group $G$ satisfies $w = 1$ if $w$ evaluates to $1$ under every substitution of elements
of $G$ for the variables. The variety of groups defined by $w = 1$ is the class of all groups
satisfying it, and a subvariety is a variety of groups contained in it.

A variety of groups is determined by its set of laws, and the sets of words that arise as the
set of all laws of a variety are exactly the sets closed under taking consequences. Hence the
subvarieties of the variety defined by $w = 1$ correspond bijectively to the closed sets of words
containing $w$, and it is these sets that are counted below.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

/-- A group `G` satisfies the identity (law) $w = 1$, where `w` is a word in the variables
$x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ (an element of the free group `FreeGroup ℕ`), if `w` evaluates to `1`
under every substitution `f : ℕ → G` of elements of `G` for the variables. -/
def SatisfiesLaw (G : Type*) [Group G] (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : ℕ → G, FreeGroup.lift f w = 1

/-- The set of all consequences of a set `S` of laws: the words `w` such that every group
satisfying all the identities $v = 1$, $v \in S$, also satisfies $w = 1$. This is the set of
all laws of the variety of groups defined by `S`. -/
def lawClosure (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Set (FreeGroup ℕ) :=
  {w | ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], (∀ v ∈ S, SatisfiesLaw G v) → SatisfiesLaw G w}

/-- A set of words `S` is the set of all laws of some variety of groups iff it is closed under
taking consequences. Varieties of groups correspond bijectively to such sets. -/
def IsVarietyLaws (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Prop :=
  lawClosure S = S

/-- The subvarieties of the variety of groups defined by the identity $w = 1$, each represented
by its set of laws. A variety is contained in the variety defined by $w = 1$ iff `w` is one of
its laws, so these are the closed sets of words containing `w`. -/
def subvarietiesOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Set (Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) :=
  {S | IsVarietyLaws S ∧ w ∈ S}

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a variety of
groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

The input of the algorithm is an identity $w = 1$, given by a word `L : List (ℕ × Bool)` in the
letters $x_i^{\pm 1}$ (`(i, true)` is $x_i$ and `(i, false)` is $x_i^{-1}$); the corresponding
element of the free group on the variables $x_0, x_1, \dots$ is `FreeGroup.mk L`, and two words
with the same image define the same identity. The algorithm has to decide whether the variety of
groups defined by $w = 1$ has at most countably many subvarieties, i.e. whether the set of its
subvarieties is countable (finite or countably infinite).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 8 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun L : List (ℕ × Bool) =>
      (subvarietiesOfLaw (FreeGroup.mk L)).Countable := by
  sorry

/-- Every group satisfies the trivial identity $1 = 1$. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_one (G : Type*) [Group G] : SatisfiesLaw G 1 := by
  simp [SatisfiesLaw]

/-- The trivial group satisfies every identity. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_of_subsingleton (G : Type*) [Group G] [Subsingleton G] (w : FreeGroup ℕ) :
    SatisfiesLaw G w :=
  fun _ => Subsingleton.elim _ _

/-- Abelian groups satisfy the commutator identity $[x_0, x_1] = 1$. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_commutator (G : Type*) [CommGroup G] :
    SatisfiesLaw G ⁅FreeGroup.of 0, FreeGroup.of 1⁆ := by
  intro f
  simp [commutatorElement_def, mul_right_comm]

/-- Every law in `S` is a consequence of `S`. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem subset_lawClosure (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : S ⊆ lawClosure S :=
  fun _ hw _ _ hS => hS _ hw

/-- Taking consequences is idempotent. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem lawClosure_lawClosure (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) :
    lawClosure (lawClosure S) = lawClosure S :=
  Set.Subset.antisymm (fun _ hw G _ hS => hw G fun _ hv => hv G hS) (subset_lawClosure _)

/-- The set of consequences of any set of laws is the set of laws of a variety. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem isVarietyLaws_lawClosure (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : IsVarietyLaws (lawClosure S) :=
  lawClosure_lawClosure S

/-- The set of all words is the set of laws of the trivial variety. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem isVarietyLaws_univ : IsVarietyLaws Set.univ :=
  Set.Subset.antisymm (Set.subset_univ _) (subset_lawClosure _)

/-- The trivial variety is a subvariety of every variety. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem univ_mem_subvarietiesOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Set.univ ∈ subvarietiesOfLaw w :=
  ⟨isVarietyLaws_univ, Set.mem_univ w⟩

/-- The variety defined by $w = 1$ is a subvariety of itself. -/
@[category test, AMS 8 20]
theorem lawClosure_singleton_mem_subvarietiesOfLaw (w : FreeGroup ℕ) :
    lawClosure {w} ∈ subvarietiesOfLaw w :=
  ⟨isVarietyLaws_lawClosure _, subset_lawClosure _ rfl⟩

end Kourovka.«8.25»
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The single-slot decomposition is correct. Minor remark: the note calls the free group of countable rank 'an encodable type'; Mathlib has no (computable) `Encodable`/`Primcodable` instance for `FreeGroup ℕ`, so the algorithm's input is taken to be the word as a list of letters (`List (ℕ × Bool)`), mapped to `FreeGroup ℕ` via `FreeGroup.mk`, which is equivalent for decidability purposes.
modeling_decisions: Input of the algorithm: an identity w = 1 is given as a word `L : List (ℕ × Bool)` in the letters x_i^{±1} (the natural syntactic encoding; `List (ℕ × Bool)` is `Primcodable`), interpreted in the free group of countably infinite rank as `FreeGroup.mk L`. The predicate depends only on `FreeGroup.mk L`. Mathlib has no computable `Primcodable (FreeGroup ℕ)` instance; deciding the predicate on arbitrary words is equivalent to deciding it on reduced words because free reduction is computable, so this is faithful to 'recognizes by an identity'. Building a `Primcodable (FreeGroup ℕ)` instance (via reduced words) would have required a nontrivial `Primrec FreeGroup.reduce` proof.
Identity as a single word w = 1 (any identity u = v is equivalent to u v⁻¹ = 1 in groups); variables indexed by ℕ (countably many variables), following the decomposition note.
A group satisfies the law w if `∀ f : ℕ → G, FreeGroup.lift f w = 1` (every substitution of group elements for the variables gives 1).

Varieties are represented by their sets of laws. `lawClosure S` is the set of consequences of S (laws of the variety defined by S), quantifying over groups `G : Type` (universe 0). Varieties correspond bijectively to closed sets (`lawClosure S = S`), and a variety is contained in the variety defined by w = 1 iff w is one of its laws; hence `subvarietiesOfLaw w = {S | lawClosure S = S ∧ w ∈ S}` is in bijection with the subvarieties. This uses only the Galois-connection formalism (no theorem such as 'varieties ↔ fully invariant subgroups of F_∞'). Restricting to universe-0 groups does not change the lattice of varieties, since the laws of a variety are determined by its countable-rank relatively free group, which lives in `Type`.
'At most countably many' is `Set.Countable` (cardinality ≤ ℵ₀, finite allowed). The variety itself and the trivial variety are counted as subvarieties (irrelevant to countability).

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 8.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity (law) is a word $w$ in the free group on the countably many variables
$x_0, x_1, \dots$; a group $G$ satisfies the identity $w = 1$ if $w$ evaluates to $1$
under every substitution of elements of $G$ for the variables. A variety of groups is
the class of all groups satisfying each identity in some set of identities, and the
variety defined by $w$ is the class of all groups satisfying $w = 1$. A subvariety of a
variety $\mathfrak{V}$ is a variety contained in $\mathfrak{V}$.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

/-- A group `G` satisfies the identity (law) `w = 1`, where `w` is a word in the free group
on the countably many variables `x₀, x₁, …`, if `w` evaluates to `1` under every substitution
of elements of `G` for the variables, i.e. under every homomorphism `FreeGroup ℕ →* G`. -/
def SatisfiesLaw (G : Type*) [Group G] (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ φ : FreeGroup ℕ →* G, φ w = 1

/-- A class of groups, i.e. a property of groups. Groups are taken in the universe `Type`; since
every variety is determined by its relatively free group of countable rank, which is countable,
this does not change the collection of subvarieties of a variety. -/
abbrev GroupClass : Type 1 := ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], Prop

/-- The variety of groups defined by a set `S` of identities: the class of all groups
satisfying every identity `w = 1` with `w ∈ S`. -/
def varietyOf (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : GroupClass :=
  fun G _ => ∀ w ∈ S, SatisfiesLaw G w

/-- A class of groups is a variety if it is the class of all groups satisfying each
identity in some set of identities. -/
def IsVariety (𝒱 : GroupClass) : Prop :=
  ∃ S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ), 𝒱 = varietyOf S

/-- The subvarieties of a class of groups `𝒱`: the varieties of groups contained in `𝒱`. -/
def subvarieties (𝒱 : GroupClass) : Set GroupClass :=
  {𝒲 | IsVariety 𝒲 ∧ ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], 𝒲 G → 𝒱 G}

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity is given to the algorithm as a word `l : List (ℕ × Bool)` in the variables
`x₀, x₁, …` and their inverses, representing the element `FreeGroup.mk l` of the free group
of countable rank. The variety it defines is the class of all groups `G` satisfying
`FreeGroup.mk l = 1`, and the question asks whether the set of its subvarieties is
countable (finite or countably infinite) for the given identity, decided by an
algorithm, i.e. whether this predicate on words is a `ComputablePred`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun l : List (ℕ × Bool) =>
      (subvarieties (varietyOf {FreeGroup.mk l})).Countable := by
  sorry

/-- Every group satisfies the trivial identity `1 = 1`. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_one (G : Type*) [Group G] : SatisfiesLaw G 1 :=
  fun φ => map_one φ

/-- The class of groups defined by a set of identities is a variety. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem isVariety_varietyOf (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : IsVariety (varietyOf S) :=
  ⟨S, rfl⟩

/-- The variety defined by the empty set of identities is the class of all groups. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem varietyOf_empty (G : Type) [Group G] : varietyOf ∅ G :=
  fun _ h => h.elim

/-- Every variety is a subvariety of itself. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem mem_subvarieties_self (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) :
    varietyOf S ∈ subvarieties (varietyOf S) :=
  ⟨isVariety_varietyOf S, fun _ _ h => h⟩

/-- A group satisfies the identity `[x₀, x₁] = 1` if and only if it is commutative. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_commutator_iff (G : Type) [Group G] :
    SatisfiesLaw G ⁅FreeGroup.of 0, FreeGroup.of 1⁆ ↔ IsMulCommutative G := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    refine ⟨⟨fun a b => ?_⟩⟩
    have := h (FreeGroup.lift fun n : ℕ => if n = 0 then a else b)
    rwa [map_commutatorElement, commutatorElement_eq_one_iff_mul_comm, FreeGroup.lift_apply_of,
      FreeGroup.lift_apply_of, if_pos rfl, if_neg one_ne_zero] at this
  · rintro ⟨⟨h⟩⟩ φ
    rw [map_commutatorElement, commutatorElement_eq_one_iff_mul_comm]

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjecture 8.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity (law) is a word $w$ in the free group $F_\infty$ on the countably many letters
$x_0, x_1, \dots$; a group $G$ satisfies it if every substitution of elements of $G$ for the
letters sends $w$ to $1$. (An identity $u = v$ is equivalent to $u v^{-1} = 1$.) The variety
of groups defined by $w$ is the class of all groups satisfying $w = 1$. A subvariety of it is a
variety of groups (a class of groups defined by a set of identities) contained in it.

A variety is determined by its set of laws, so the subvarieties of the variety defined by $w$
correspond bijectively to the closed sets of laws $L \subseteq F_\infty$ containing $w$, where
$L$ is closed if every law holding in all groups satisfying $L$ already lies in $L$. Hence the
variety defined by $w$ has at most countably many subvarieties iff the set of closed sets of
laws containing $w$ is countable. The question asks whether this property of $w$ is decidable.

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

open FreeGroup

section Primcodable

variable {α : Type*} [Primcodable α] [DecidableEq α]

/-- Free reduction of words is primitive recursive. -/
@[category API, AMS 3 20]
theorem primrec_reduce : Primrec (reduce : List (α × Bool) → List (α × Bool)) := by
  have hh : Primrec fun x : ((α × Bool) × List (α × Bool) × List (α × Bool)) ×
      (α × Bool) × List (α × Bool) =>
      if x.1.1.1 = x.2.1.1 ∧ x.1.1.2 = !x.2.1.2 then x.2.2 else x.1.1 :: x.2.1 :: x.2.2 := by
    refine Primrec.ite (PrimrecPred.and ?_ ?_) ?_ ?_
    · exact Primrec.eq.comp (Primrec.fst.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.fst))
        (Primrec.fst.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.snd))
    · exact Primrec.eq.comp (Primrec.snd.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.fst))
        (Primrec.not.comp (Primrec.snd.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.snd)))
    · exact Primrec.snd.comp Primrec.snd
    · exact Primrec.list_cons.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.fst)
        (Primrec.list_cons.comp (Primrec.fst.comp Primrec.snd) (Primrec.snd.comp Primrec.snd))
  have hstep : Primrec fun p : (α × Bool) × List (α × Bool) × List (α × Bool) =>
      List.casesOn (motive := fun _ => List (α × Bool)) p.2.2 [p.1] fun hd tl =>
        if p.1.1 = hd.1 ∧ p.1.2 = !hd.2 then tl else p.1 :: hd :: tl :=
    Primrec.list_casesOn (Primrec.snd.comp Primrec.snd)
      (Primrec.list_cons.comp Primrec.fst (Primrec.const [])) hh.to₂
  exact (Primrec.list_rec Primrec.id (Primrec.const []) (hstep.comp Primrec.snd).to₂).of_eq
    fun L => rfl

/-- The free group on a `Primcodable` type is `Primcodable`, via reduced words. -/
instance : Primcodable (FreeGroup α) :=
  haveI : Primcodable {L : List (α × Bool) // reduce L = L} :=
    Primcodable.subtype (Primrec.eq.comp primrec_reduce Primrec.id)
  Primcodable.ofEquiv {L : List (α × Bool) // reduce L = L}
    { toFun := fun w => ⟨toWord w, reduce_toWord w⟩
      invFun := fun L => mk L.1
      left_inv := fun _ => mk_toWord
      right_inv := fun L => Subtype.ext (toWord_mk.trans L.2) }

end Primcodable

/-- A group `G` satisfies the identity (law) `w = 1`, where `w` is a word in the free group on
the countably many letters `x₀, x₁, …`, if every substitution of elements of `G` for the letters
sends `w` to `1`. -/
def SatisfiesLaw (G : Type*) [Group G] (w : FreeGroup ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : ℕ → G, lift f w = 1

/-- The set of all laws of the variety of groups defined by a set `S` of identities: the words
`u` such that `u = 1` holds in every group satisfying all identities in `S`.

Quantifying only over groups in `Type` loses no generality: laws pass to subgroups, and a
countably generated group in any universe is isomorphic to a group in `Type`. -/
def lawsOfVariety (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Set (FreeGroup ℕ) :=
  {u | ∀ (G : Type) [Group G], (∀ v ∈ S, SatisfiesLaw G v) → SatisfiesLaw G u}

/-- `L` is the full set of laws of some variety of groups, i.e. `L` is closed under consequence.
Since a variety of groups is determined by its set of laws, the varieties of groups correspond
bijectively to the sets `L` with `IsLawsOfVariety L`, and the subvarieties of the variety
defined by `w` correspond to those with `w ∈ L`. -/
def IsLawsOfVariety (L : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Prop :=
  lawsOfVariety L = L

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes by an identity whether it defines a
variety of groups that has at most countably many subvarieties?

Here the identity is `w = 1` for a word `w` in the free group on countably many letters. The
subvarieties of the variety defined by `w` correspond bijectively to the closed sets of laws
`L` with `w ∈ L`, so the variety has at most countably many subvarieties iff the set of such
`L` is countable. The answer is "yes" iff this predicate on `w` is computable.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun w : FreeGroup ℕ =>
      {L : Set (FreeGroup ℕ) | IsLawsOfVariety L ∧ w ∈ L}.Countable := by
  sorry

/-- Every group satisfies the trivial law `1 = 1`. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_one (G : Type*) [Group G] : SatisfiesLaw G 1 := by
  simp [SatisfiesLaw]

/-- Commutative groups satisfy the commutator law `[x₀, x₁] = 1`. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem satisfiesLaw_commutator (G : Type*) [CommGroup G] : SatisfiesLaw G ⁅of 0, of 1⁆ := by
  intro f
  rw [map_commutatorElement, commutatorElement_eq_one_iff_mul_comm]
  exact mul_comm _ _

/-- Every identity in `S` is a law of the variety defined by `S`. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem subset_lawsOfVariety (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) : S ⊆ lawsOfVariety S :=
  fun _ hu _ _ hG => hG _ hu

/-- The set of laws of the variety defined by `S` is closed under consequence. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem isLawsOfVariety_lawsOfVariety (S : Set (FreeGroup ℕ)) :
    IsLawsOfVariety (lawsOfVariety S) := by
  refine Set.Subset.antisymm (fun u hu G _ hG => hu G ?_) (subset_lawsOfVariety _)
  exact fun v hv => hv G hG

/-- The set of all words is the set of laws of the trivial variety. -/
@[category test, AMS 20]
theorem isLawsOfVariety_univ : IsLawsOfVariety Set.univ :=
  Set.eq_univ_of_univ_subset (subset_lawsOfVariety _)

end Kourovka.«8.25»

Here the identity is `w = 1` for a word `w` in the free group on countably many letters. The
subvarieties of the variety defined by `w` correspond bijectively to the closed sets of laws
`L` with `w ∈ L`, so the variety has at most countably many subvarieties iff the set of such
`L` is countable. The answer is "yes" iff this predicate on `w` is computable.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 3 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun w : FreeGroup ℕ =>
      {L : Set (FreeGroup ℕ) | IsLawsOfVariety L ∧ w ∈ L}.Countable := by
  sorry

/-!
# Conjecture 8.25

by A. V. Kuznetsov

Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes from an identity whether it defines a variety of
groups with at most countably many subvarieties?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

/-- A subgroup of the free group of countable rank is fully invariant if every endomorphism maps
it into itself. -/
def IsFullyInvariant (N : Subgroup (FreeGroup ℕ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : FreeGroup ℕ →* FreeGroup ℕ, N ≤ N.comap f

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which, given a group identity, recognizes whether the variety of
groups defined by that identity has at most countably many subvarieties?

An identity is encoded by a finite word `w` in countably many variables, and `FreeGroup.mk w` is
the corresponding element of the free group. By the correspondence between varieties of groups
and fully invariant subgroups of the free group of countable rank, the subvarieties of the variety
defined by $w = 1$ correspond to the fully invariant subgroups containing `FreeGroup.mk w`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun w : List (ℕ × Bool) ↦
      Cardinal.mk {N : Subgroup (FreeGroup ℕ) //
        IsFullyInvariant N ∧ FreeGroup.mk w ∈ N} ≤ Cardinal.aleph0 := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«8.25»
modeling_decisions: A group identity is represented by a primitively codable finite word `List (ℕ × Bool)` in countably many variables; `FreeGroup.mk` sends this code to the corresponding element of the free group. The predicate depends only on that element, not on the chosen word representative.
Subvarieties are counted through Birkhoff's correspondence: they correspond bijectively to fully invariant subgroups of `FreeGroup ℕ` containing the given identity.
“At most countably many” is expressed by `Cardinal.mk … ≤ Cardinal.aleph0`, including finite cardinalities.
Existence of an algorithm is expressed by Mathlib's `ComputablePred`; consequently `answer(True)` denotes a positive answer.

new_definitions.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib has `Submodule.IsFullyInvariant` for submodules, but no corresponding definition for subgroups; the submodule definition is not applicable to the free group.
new_definitions.name: Kourovka.«8.25».IsFullyInvariant
new_definitions.why_needed: The statement needs the group-theoretic notion of a subgroup stable under every endomorphism in order to represent sets of laws and hence subvarieties.

/-!

by A. V. Kuznetsov

variety of groups that it defines has at most countably many subvarieties?

*Reference:* [The Kourovka Notebook](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.0300v46)
-/

namespace Kourovka.«8.25»

/-- A subgroup of a group is fully invariant if every endomorphism maps it
into itself. -/
def IsFullyInvariant {G : Type*} [Group G] (N : Subgroup G) : Prop :=
  ∀ f : G →* G, N.map f ≤ N

/--
Does there exist an algorithm which recognizes, given a group identity,
whether the variety of groups defined by that identity has at most countably
many subvarieties?

An identity is encoded by a finite word in countably many variables and is
interpreted as an element of `FreeGroup ℕ`. By the correspondence between
group varieties and fully invariant subgroups of the countably generated free
group, the subvarieties of the variety defined by $w = 1$ correspond to the
fully invariant subgroups that contain $w$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 20]
theorem kourovka.«8.25» : answer(sorry) ↔
    ComputablePred fun w : List (ℕ × Bool) =>
      Set.Countable {N : Subgroup (FreeGroup ℕ) |
        IsFullyInvariant N ∧ FreeGroup.mk w ∈ N} := by
  sorry

end Kourovka.«8.25»
modeling_decisions: Encoded an input identity as a finite word `List (ℕ × Bool)` and interpreted it using `FreeGroup.mk`; this gives the standard computable presentation of elements of the countably generated free group without requiring a missing `Primcodable (FreeGroup ℕ)` instance.
Used the Birkhoff correspondence: subvarieties of the variety defined by `w = 1` correspond to fully invariant subgroups of `FreeGroup ℕ` containing `w`.
Used `Set.Countable` for “at most countably many,” so finite collections are included.
Used `ComputablePred` to express existence of an algorithm deciding the property from the encoded identity.

new_definitions.why_needed: The statement is represented through the standard correspondence between group varieties and fully invariant subgroups, requiring invariance under every group endomorphism.
